plan: Literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000053), an original story: a teenager begins beating a grandfather at chess, notices a move the grandfather taught them never to make, tests the grandfather with an unguarded queen, and chooses not to learn the answer. No chess or grandparent passage in the ACT Reading bank. Ten questions, four aimed at hard (significance of a move, interpreting stated ambiguity, unstated motive for gratitude, closing detail). Items made gender-neutral before review after the first blind pair noted the passage never states the narrator's gender; all ten re-solved. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The Unguarded Queen
passages.text:
Every Sunday since I was eight, my grandfather and I had played chess at the card table by his window. He never let me win. When I was nine and cried after losing my queen, he handed me a tissue and said, "A piece you leave unguarded is a piece you have given away," and then he took my rook. I hated him a little that afternoon. By the time I was twelve, I could repeat the sentence along with him.

The spring I turned fifteen, I began to win. The first time, I thought it was luck. The second time, I thought I had finally learned something. By the fifth time, I had started telling my friends at school that I could beat my grandfather, a man who had once played in tournaments, and I liked the way they looked at me when I said it.

Then, in early May, he moved his bishop to a square where my knight could take it for nothing. I stared at the board. It was exactly the kind of move he had spent seven years teaching me never to make. I took the bishop, and he nodded as if I had done something sensible, and twenty minutes later I won again.

That night I lay awake replaying the game. There were only two explanations I could think of, and I did not like either of them. Either he was letting me win, which meant that every victory I had bragged about was a gift, or he was no longer seeing the board the way he used to, which meant something I did not want to name.

The next Sunday I decided to find out. Halfway through the game, I left my queen where his knight could take it—a mistake so plain that the nine-year-old version of me would have seen it. I kept my eyes on the board and waited.

He looked at the queen for a long time. His hand moved toward the knight, stopped, and settled on a pawn instead, which he pushed forward one square. Then he looked up at me, and I could not tell whether his expression was kind or confused, or whether there was any difference.

I could have asked him. The question was right there, as plain as the unguarded queen. Instead I moved my queen to safety, and we played on, and I lost, and I was more grateful for that loss than for any of my wins. When we finished, I set the pieces back on their starting squares the way he had taught me, white on the right, and asked whether he wanted to play again next week.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best summarizes the passage?

choices.A: A teenager finally masters the chess strategy a grandfather taught and wins a local tournament.
choices.B: A teenager's pride in beating a grandfather gives way to uncertainty about what the wins really mean.
choices.C: A grandfather admits to his grandchild that he has been losing their chess games on purpose.
choices.D: A grandchild decides to stop playing chess with the grandfather after discovering a painful truth.

candidates.evidence: There were only two explanations I could think of, and I did not like either of them.
candidates.explanation: The narrator begins proud of the wins, notices a careless move, tests the grandfather, and is left unsure whether the wins were gifts or signs of decline.

A.rationale: No tournament is mentioned for the narrator; the grandfather once played in them.

C.rationale: The grandfather never explains anything; the narrator chooses not to ask.

D.rationale: The narrator asks to play again next week, and the narrator never confirms the truth.

hints: How does the narrator feel about winning at the start and at the end?

strategy.explanation: Trace the narrator's feelings from beginning to end.

candidates.remember: A summary must cover the turn in the story, not just its opening.

candidates.stem: The details in the first paragraph mainly establish that, when the narrator was younger, the narrator's grandfather was:

choices.A: a strict teacher who expected the narrator to learn from mistakes.
choices.B: an impatient player who rarely explained his moves.
choices.C: a gentle player who often let the narrator take back bad moves.
choices.D: a distant relative the narrator saw only on a few special occasions.

candidates.explanation: The grandfather never let the narrator win, offered a lesson about unguarded pieces, and then took the rook: firm, but teaching.

B.rationale: He did explain, in the sentence about unguarded pieces.

C.rationale: "He never let me win," and he took the rook right after the lesson.

D.rationale: They played every Sunday for years.

hints: What does the grandfather do right after offering the tissue?

strategy.explanation: Use the tissue and the rook together.

candidates.remember: Characterization comes from what a character does as well as says.

candidates.stem: The narrator is troubled by the bishop move described in the third paragraph mainly because the move:

choices.A: costs the narrator a valuable piece early in the game.
choices.B: shows that the grandfather has learned a new strategy.
choices.C: breaks a rule the grandfather had long insisted on.
choices.D: lets the grandfather win the game in only twenty minutes.

candidates.evidence: It was exactly the kind of move he had spent seven years teaching me never to make.
candidates.explanation: Leaving the bishop to be taken for nothing is exactly what the grandfather taught the narrator never to do, so the move is out of character.

A.rationale: It is the grandfather's bishop that is lost, not the narrator's piece.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests a new strategy; the move is a basic mistake.

D.rationale: The narrator, not the grandfather, wins twenty minutes later.

hints: Why would this particular move surprise the narrator?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence right after "I stared at the board."

candidates.remember: Look for the detail that ties a later event back to an earlier lesson.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect the move to the earlier lesson and avoid misreading whose piece was lost.

candidates.stem: The narrator leaves the queen unguarded in the fifth paragraph mainly in order to:

choices.A: give the grandfather a win to make up for the earlier losses.
choices.B: show the grandfather that the narrator no longer needs lessons.
choices.C: test a new strategy, read about somewhere, for sacrificing the queen.
choices.D: see whether the grandfather would notice and punish the mistake.

candidates.evidence: The next Sunday I decided to find out.
candidates.explanation: After lying awake over two possible explanations, the narrator sets a test: a mistake so plain that any attentive player would punish it.

A.rationale: The narrator says, "I decided to find out," not that the goal was to give a win.

B.rationale: A deliberate blunder would not show this.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests a planned sacrifice strategy.

hints: What did the narrator want to find out?

strategy.explanation: Connect paragraph 5 to the two explanations in paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: A character's action often answers a question raised just before it.

candidates.stem: As it is used in the seventh paragraph, the word plain most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: as plain as the unguarded queen
candidates.explanation: The question was as plain as the unguarded queen, which was a mistake "so plain" a child would see it, so "plain" means "obvious."

A.rationale: The question is not about style or decoration.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the question is ugly.

D.rationale: "Plain" here does not describe a surface.

hints: What does "plain" mean when describing the unguarded queen?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word from the queen comparison.

candidates.remember: Read the comparison the word is part of.

candidates.stem: Based on the sixth paragraph, the narrator's view of the grandfather's response to the unguarded queen is best described as:

choices.A: uncertain, since the response could reflect either kindness or confusion.
choices.B: relieved, because the grandfather clearly saw the mistake and chose mercy.
choices.C: alarmed, because the grandfather clearly failed to see the queen at all.
choices.D: annoyed, because the grandfather refused to take the game seriously.

candidates.evidence: I could not tell whether his expression was kind or confused
candidates.explanation: The narrator explicitly cannot tell whether the expression was kind or confused, so the narrator's view is uncertain.

B.rationale: The narrator "could not tell" which it was.

C.rationale: The grandfather looked at the queen "for a long time"; nothing is clear.

hints: What does the narrator say could not be told?

strategy.explanation: Find the last sentence of paragraph 6.

candidates.remember: When a narrator says "I could not tell," avoid answers that claim certainty.

author_checklist.hardness: Two distractors each pick one interpretation and present it as clear.

candidates.stem: The fourth paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: describe the game in which the narrator first beat the grandfather.
choices.B: explain why the grandfather stopped playing in chess tournaments.
choices.C: lay out the two possibilities that the narrator then sets out to test.
choices.D: reveal that the narrator's friends doubted the narrator's claims about chess.

candidates.evidence: Either he was letting me win
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 states the two explanations, and paragraph 5 begins the test: "The next Sunday I decided to find out."

A.rationale: The first win is mentioned in paragraph 2.

B.rationale: Tournaments are mentioned only in passing in paragraph 2.

D.rationale: The friends are in paragraph 2, and they are impressed.

hints: What does paragraph 5 decide to find out?

strategy.explanation: Look at what the next paragraph does with paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: A paragraph's function often shows in how the next paragraph uses it.

candidates.stem: The narrator describes being "more grateful for that loss than for any of my wins" most likely because the loss:

choices.A: proved that the grandfather had been letting the narrator win all spring.
choices.B: showed that the narrator had finally become the better of the two players.
choices.C: meant that the narrator could stop bragging to friends about chess.
choices.D: let the narrator avoid a feared answer and keep their games going.

candidates.explanation: By saving the queen and losing, the narrator ends the test without an answer, sparing himself both possibilities and keeping the Sunday games as they were.

A.rationale: The loss proves nothing; the narrator still does not know.

B.rationale: Losing does not show the narrator is the better player.

C.rationale: The friends are not mentioned at the end, and losing does not affect the bragging.

hints: What does the narrator choose not to do just before the loss?

strategy.explanation: Connect "I could have asked him" to the gratitude.

candidates.remember: A character's gratitude can come from what they avoided, not what they gained.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must infer an unstated motive from the decision not to ask.

candidates.stem: The detail that the narrator set the pieces back "the way he had taught me, white on the right" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show the narrator honoring the grandfather's lessons and their routine.
choices.B: suggest that the narrator has forgotten some of the basic rules of chess.
choices.C: reveal that the grandfather is unable to set up the board himself.
choices.D: indicate that the narrator plans to stop playing chess after this game.

candidates.evidence: the way he had taught me, white on the right
candidates.explanation: Resetting the board exactly as the grandfather taught, then asking to play next week, shows the narrator preserving the lessons and the ritual.

B.rationale: The narrator sets the pieces up correctly, as taught.

C.rationale: The narrator sets up the board, but nothing says the grandfather cannot.

D.rationale: The narrator immediately asks to play again next week.

hints: How does this detail connect to the rest of the final paragraph?

strategy.explanation: Read the detail together with the invitation that follows.

candidates.remember: Closing details often echo earlier ones to show what a character values.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must read a small action as an expression of the narrator's choice.

candidates.stem: The passage is told from the point of view of:

choices.A: the grandfather, explaining why he began to lose on purpose.
choices.B: an outside narrator who knows what both characters are thinking.
choices.C: the grandchild, looking back on events from the spring of turning fifteen.
choices.D: one of the narrator's school friends who heard about the games.

candidates.evidence: The spring I turned fifteen, I began to win.
candidates.explanation: The "I" is the grandchild, recounting the spring of turning fifteen in past tense, with no access to the grandfather's thoughts.

A.rationale: The narrator is the grandchild; the grandfather never explains.

B.rationale: The narrator cannot tell what the grandfather is thinking.

D.rationale: The friends appear only briefly and do not narrate.

strategy.explanation: Identify the narrator and what the narrator can and cannot know.

candidates.remember: A first-person narrator cannot know what other characters think.
